findings.description: The "Research messages" annual series presents a summary of the research-focused reports produced by the National Centre for Vocational Education Research (NCVER) each year. In addition to presenting the research reports published by NCVER during 2016, NCVER has expanded this edition to include other relevant and informative resources, including summaries, infographics and statistical papers. A key focus area of this research is the learning needs and educational pathways of students, who are at the heart of the VET system, and supporting individuals and organisations to make informed choices in skills development through the VET system. Based on the research prospectus, NCVER has organized their research program into four priority areas: (1) Productivity; (2) Participation and outcomes; (3) Teaching and learning; and (4) The place and role of VET. The following provides summaries of projects that were published under each of these priorities. They include: (1) Beyond mentoring: social support structures for young Australian carpentry apprentices (John Buchanan, Catherine Raffaele, Nick Glozier and Aran Kanagaratnam); (2) Costs and benefits of education and training for the economy, business and individuals (Tabatha Griffin); (3) Cross-occupational skill transferability: challenges and opportunities in a changing economy (Darryn Snell, Victor Gekara and Krystle Gatt); (4) Defining "STEM" skills: review and synthesis of the literature (Gitta Siekmann & Patrick Korbel); (5) Evaluation framework measuring return on investment (ROI) in TVET (Jane Schueler); (6) Firms' motivation for training apprentices: an Australian-German comparison (Harald Pfeifer); (7) The Australian literacy and numeracy workforce: a literature review. Foundation Skills Literature Review Project (Joanne Medlin); (8) Exploring perspectives on adult language, literacy and numeracy: foundation skills literature review project (Daniella Mayer); (9) Foundation skills policy contexts and measures of impact: foundation skills literature review project (Jane Newton); (10) The salience of diversity in foundation skills contexts, pedagogies and research: foundation skills Literature review project (Lynda Cameron); (11) Measuring STEM in vocational education and training (Patrick Korbel); (12) Providing social support for apprentices: good practice guide (NCVER); (13) What is STEM? The need for unpacking its definitions and applications (Gitta Siekmann); (14) When one door closes: VET's role in helping displaced workers find jobs (Bridget Wibrow and Michelle Circelli); (15) Work-based learning and work-integrated learning: fostering engagement with employers (Georgina Atkinson); (16) Can VET help create a more inclusive society? (Hielke Buddelmeyer and Cain Polidano); (17) The impact of disadvantage on VET completion and employment gaps (Duncan McVicar and Domenico Tabasso); (18) Increasing survey engagement through gamification and the use of mobile devices (Maree Ackehurst and Rose-Anne Polvere); (19) Shedding light: private "for profit" training providers and young early school leavers (George Myconos, Kira Clarke and Kitty Te Riele); (20) Uptake and utility of VET qualifications (Patrick Korbel and Josie Misko); (21) VET program completion rates: an evaluation of the current method (NCVER); (22) Graduate programs for VET students: is there a need? (Bridget Wibrow and Laura Jackson); (23) Apprenticeships and vocations: assessing the impact of research on policy and practice (Jo Hargreaves); (24) The development of Australia's national training system: a dynamic tension between consistency and flexibility (Kaye Bowman and Suzy McKenna); (25) Jurisdictional approaches to student training entitlements: commonalities and differences (Kaye Bowman and Suzy McKenna); (26) Making sense of total VET activity: an initial market analysis (Alison Anlezark and Paul Foley); (27) Student entitlement models in Australia's national training system: expert views (Kaye Bowman and Suzy McKenna); (28) Trends in VET: policy and participation (Georgina Atkinson and John Stanwick); (29) VET provider market structures: history, growth and change (Patrick Korbel and Josie Misko); (30) 24th National Vocational Education and Training Research Conference "no frills": refereed papers (Laura Jackson, Ed.); (31) Improving VET teachers' skills and their approach to professional learning 24th National Vocational Education and Training Research Conference "no frills": refereed paper (Anne Dening); (32) Learning preferences of Enrolled Nursing students: Educational preparation and training for workplace readiness. 24th National Vocational Education and Training Research Conference "no frills": refereed paper (Kalpana Raghunathan, Sonia Allen and Elisabeth Jacob); (33) Profiling the institutional diversity of VET providers in Australia, across four broad dimensions 24th National Vocational Education and Training Research Conference "no frills": refereed paper (Peter Bentley, Leo Goedegebuure and Ruth Schubert); (34) Skills needed for innovation: a review. 24th National Vocational Education and Training Research Conference "no frills": refereed paper (Michael Walsh); (35) Understanding the needs of VET students articulating to second-year university 24th National Vocational Education and Training Research Conference "no frills": refereed Paper (Mark Symmons, Paul Kremer and Alvin Rendell); I had worried in advance about the idea of being part of a tour group, and in fact I would have spent more time in the Museum of Egyptian Antiquities than our guide permitted us. Ro- berto, our other waiter, remembering my preference for mint tea, had it steeping before I ordered it. After dinner, I could have danced and been entertained in all of the ship's three night- clubs. I could have seen a movie, watched tanned, beautifully dressed South Americans play blackjack in the casino, or had quiet drinks in a big low leather chair high up in the Windjammer Room. But I was feeling fortu- nate to be on a cruise ship in the Mediterra- nean, so I strolled out on the Promenade Deck instead, to see how fast the ship was going and to watch the reflection the moon made on the dark water. The next day, in Jerusalem, we saw the Wailing Wall and the Church of the Holy Sep- ulchre, and were moved by the Biblical land- scape that surrounds the city-dark sand hills ringed with white stone terraces and dotted with olive trees. In the bazaar in the Old City, there were beautiful old silk embroidered robes and silver bracelets to bargain for, as well as lambskin slippers, copper and brass souvenirs. As our bus passed by one souvenir stand, the proprietor called out to us, "Every- thing for nothing." Though he meant it as a come-on, he sounded as if that was what he - thought Americans expected to get. Actually, "everything for nothing" was a fair description of what ship life felt like. Food was available at almost any hour; a bar was always open somewhere. When they weren't lazing, passengers were most likely to be acting as consumers in one form or another. Eating was the major pastime at sea, and some of the biggest occasions on board ship had to do with food. That af- ternoon we shopped in the port city of Kusa- dasi for jewelry, Turkish carpets, copper, and sweaters. findings.title: Greece with the Cyclades & Northern Sporades
creator: great britain. foreign office. historical section
description: In preparation for the peace conference that was expected to follow World War I, in the spring of 1917 the British Foreign Office established a special section responsible for preparing background information for use by British delegates to the conference. Greece with the Cyclades & Northern Sporades is Number 18 in a series of more than 160 studies produced by the section, most of which were published after the conclusion of the 1919 Paris Peace Conference. The book covers physical and political geography, political history, social and political conditions, and economic conditions. The part on political history focuses on the period between the War of Independence (1821-29), in which Greece secured its independence from the Ottoman Empire, and the First and Second Balkan Wars (1912-13), by which Greece acquired lands from Bulgaria and Turkey that nearly doubled its territory and population. The Cyclades and the Northern Sporades are islands in the Aegean Sea that came under Greek control during the Balkan Wars, but whose incorporation into Greece had not yet been formally recognized by the Great Powers. The appendix includes the texts of important documents relating to Greece in the 19th century. These include the Protocol of London of March 22, 1829, in which the Great Powers of Britain, France, and Russia guaranteed the status of Greece as an autonomous entity under the suzerainty of the Ottoman Empire; the Protocol of London of February 3, 1830, in which the same three powers guaranteed Greece's status as a fully independent kingdom; and the Treaty of London of March 29, 1864, in which Greece gained sovereignty over the Ionian Islands, a British protectorate since 1815. Greece was at first neutral during World War I, but it entered the war on the side of Britain and France in June 1917. Greece's involvement in the war itself is not covered in this study. findings.title: The Recovery Kernel
findings.creator: J R TOKEN
findings.description: 🧬 THE RECOVERY KERNEL A systems-architecture framework for understanding addiction, behavior, biological bottlenecks, and recovery. Forkable. Global. Human-first. Insight, not instructions. Clarity, not prescriptions. Understanding, not judgment. The Problem Was Never That People Were Broken For generations, addiction has been explained through competing languages: moral failure , lack of willpower , disease , trauma , bad choices , genetics , environment , brain chemistry . Each of these lenses may contain part of the picture. But people are systems. Human behavior emerges from interactions between biology, environment, learning, memory, stress, reward, metabolism, expression, social context, and time. The Recovery Kernel was built to study those interactions together. It is an open-source systems framework for exploring the architecture behind addictive patterns and recovery. The central premise is simple: Do not begin with blame. Begin with architecture. 🎯 What Is The Recovery Kernel? The Recovery Kernel is a home-level biological and behavioral insight framework designed to help people explore: why addictive patterns may emerge; how those patterns become reinforced; why people can respond differently to similar substances or environments; how biology and lived experience may interact; where biological or behavioral bottlenecks may exist; and why recovery pathways can differ dramatically between individuals. The Kernel does not replace clinicians, therapists, laboratories, emergency services, or medical systems. It gives individuals another tool: a structured way to ask better questions. The framework brings together areas such as: 🧬 genetic architecture 🧠 neurochemical signaling and clearance 🔄 behavioral reinforcement loops 🌍 environmental conditioning 🧪 metabolism and pharmacology 🧫 epigenetic and regulatory factors 🎭 expressive and behavioral tendencies 🧩 lived experience and contextual signals The goal is not to reduce a human being to a gene, diagnosis, substance, or story. The goal is to construct a more complete map. 🧠 Why This Exists Most people trying to understand addiction are caught between three worlds. The clinical world Accurate information can be buried inside terminology that many people were never taught to interpret. The anecdotal world Forums and social media overflow with: “This worked for me.” “Take this.” “Never take that.” “You have exactly what I had.” Personal experience can be valuable. But one person's nervous system is not everyone else's nervous system. The lived world Then there is the person's actual experience: Why does this affect me differently? Why can that person stop and I cannot? Why do I repeat something I consciously want to stop? Why does my behavior change under stress? Why do I feel like three different versions of myself depending on my state? Why does the explanation I was given not seem to fit everything I experience? The Recovery Kernel exists in the space between these worlds. It provides a structured lens for asking: What interacting systems could produce this pattern? It is not a treatment. It is not a diagnosis. It is not a medical protocol. It is a framework for understanding. ⚙️ Addiction as a Systems Bottleneck Traditional narratives frequently isolate one explanation: the substance or the trauma or the genes or the environment or the behavior The Kernel asks a different question: What happens when several individually manageable constraints interact and become one reinforcing system? A simplified conceptual model might look like this: GENETIC ARCHITECTURE ↓ SIGNALING + CLEARANCE ↓ REWARD / STRESS RESPONSE ↕ ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONING ↕ BEHAVIORAL REINFORCEMENT ↕ MEMORY + EXPRESSION ↓ REPEATING SYSTEM STATE The point is not that every addictive pattern follows this exact sequence. The point is that human behavior is multivariable . The Kernel treats addictive patterns as possible system-level bottlenecks rather than evidence of bad character. 🪞 The Kernel Is a Mirror The Recovery Kernel is designed to help a person examine their own patterns without immediately converting observation into condemnation. It asks questions such as: What happened? Under what conditions? What changed before the behavior? Which state was the person in? Which signals are consistent? Which signals contradict one another? What information is missing? What could be biological? What could be environmental? What could be learned? What could be temporary? What requires professional investigation? The Kernel does not say: “You are broken.” It asks: “What architecture could explain what you are experiencing?” 🎭 Why Bias Matters Human testimony is extraordinarily valuable. It is also variable. People report their experiences from different system states: optimized states; dysregulated states; masked states; defensive states; performative states; confused states; fatigued states; intoxicated states; withdrawal states; socially filtered states. A person can minimize. A person can exaggerate. A person can forget. A person can reinterpret the past through the present. A person can answer with what they believe they should feel rather than what they actually felt. Sometimes people simply do not know which details are relevant. For this reason: Phenotype-first inference is probabilistic, not deterministic. The Kernel does not automatically treat testimony as objective truth. It treats testimony as signal . Expression is not dismissed as noise. Behavior is not automatically converted into diagnosis. Signals are considered: carefully, contextually, comparatively, and with explicit awareness of uncertainty. 🧬 Genomic Data: Powerful, but Optional The Recovery Kernel can be explored without genomic sequencing. In this mode, it operates as a probabilistic reasoning framework . It can help organize questions around: behavioral patterns; environmental triggers; family history; differential substance response; medication history; recurring states; tolerance patterns; recovery patterns; expressive tendencies. When high-quality genomic information is available, the framework can incorporate a more detailed architectural layer. Depending on the quality and type of data available, genomic analysis may examine areas including: metabolic pathways; receptor variants; transporter architecture; regulatory regions; methylation-related pathways; copy-number variation; pharmacogenomic markers; clearance pathways; signaling architecture. High-coverage whole-genome sequencing data can provide substantially more information than phenotype inference alone. But genomic information is not magical. It still requires interpretation. Genetics is not destiny. And the Kernel remains: educational, exploratory, and non-diagnostic. 🔬 What Makes The Recovery Kernel Different? Many recovery resources are primarily: Therapeutic 12-step programs, psychotherapy, CBT, counseling, group work, and related interventions. Anecdotal Stories and personal recommendations based on individual experience. Clinical Research papers, diagnostic manuals, pharmacology references, and professional medical systems. The Recovery Kernel occupies another layer. It is a systems-engineering model of human behavior. It was developed through an evolving collaboration involving: human design and lived observation; software systems; structured knowledge models; multiple artificial-intelligence systems; genomic and pharmacological reasoning frameworks; document libraries; translation systems; open-source iteration. Its philosophical orientation is: Move Away From Move Toward Moral judgment Systems understanding Shame Architecture Certainty without evidence Explicit uncertainty One-size-fits-all narratives Individual context Anecdotal absolutism Structured evidence Stigma Understanding “What is wrong with you?” “What happened in this system?” 🏠 What Can Someone Do With It at Home? The Kernel is intended to help people explore and understand . A person can use the framework to: 🧠 explore mechanisms that may contribute to addictive patterns; 🧬 examine possible relationships between biology and behavior; 🔁 map repeating behavioral loops; 🌍 identify environmental contexts associated with increased vulnerability; 🧪 better understand why substances may affect individuals differently; 📊 organize observations before speaking with professionals; 🔎 compare lived experience with clinical explanations; 💊 explore questions to discuss with pharmacists or physicians; 🧩 contextualize contradictory experiences; 🪞 examine behavior through a biological and systems lens rather than a moral one. It gives people insight, not instructions. Clarity, not prescriptions. Understanding, not treatment. 🌅 What This Gives People Before having a structured framework, many people experience: shame confusion contradictory advice anecdotal noise opaque clinical language fragmented explanations difficulty reconciling lived experience with expert opinion The Kernel attempts to replace that fragmentation with: a structured, bias-aware model; a vocabulary for discussing architecture; a way to organize observations; a method for evaluating competing explanations; a way to better prepare for conversations with professionals; a means of seeing tendencies without immediately converting them into identity; a way to remove unnecessary moral framing from biological and behavioral questions. For many people, the most important question is not: “What should I be called?” It is: “Why does this keep happening?” The Recovery Kernel was built around that question. 🔊 Built for the Global Dancefloor The Recovery Kernel was not built only for clinics, offices, or quiet rooms. It was also built with the global dancefloor in mind. For the person standing beneath a speaker stack at 4:00 in the morning. For the person flying home on Monday wondering why their friends seem fine and they do not. For the person who loves music, movement, travel, nightlife, community, and altered states — but wants to understand their own biology well enough to protect the life that makes those experiences possible. For DJs. For dancers. For bartenders. For promoters. For queer nightlife communities. For sober ravers. For people in recovery who still love electronic music. For people who do not identify with traditional recovery culture at all. For the friends who notice something is wrong before anyone else does. For the people who dance all night and still have to wake up inside the same nervous system the next morning. 🌍 The Communities We Had in Mind The Recovery Kernel is designed to be relevant to people moving through the international electronic-music, festival, rave, club, circuit, techno, house, psytrance, and sound-system communities surrounding scenes and events such as: 🇳🇱 Amsterdam & The Netherlands Amsterdam Dance Event — ADE Awakenings Dekmantel DGTL Mysteryland 🇩🇪 Berlin & Germany Time Warp Fusion Festival Nature One Airbeat One Rave The Planet And the wider Berlin club ecosystem. 🇺🇸 Miami Ultra Music Festival Miami Music Week And the wider after-hours ecosystem surrounding Club Space and Miami dance culture. 🇬🇪 Tbilisi & Georgia 4GB Tbilisi Open Air And the wider Tbilisi electronic-music and underground club community. 🇨🇴 Bogotá & Medellín BAUM Festival Ritvales And the rapidly growing Colombian house and techno communities surrounding Bogotá and Medellín. 🇵🇱 Poland Unsound Audioriver And the club and experimental electronic communities of Warsaw, Kraków, and the wider Polish scene. 🇷🇸 Belgrade & Serbia No Sleep Festival Along with the wider Belgrade and Serbian electronic-music ecosystem. 🇦🇱 Albania UNUM Festival Kala Festival And the growing electronic-music communities of the Albanian Riviera. 🇬🇧 London Junction 2 Body Movements Along with London's house, techno, queer, underground, and sound-system communities. 🇫🇷 Paris The Peacock Society Along with the broader Paris electronic and underground nightlife community. 🇪🇸 Ibiza The wider Ibiza dance-music ecosystem: International Music Summit — IMS Circoloco DC-10 and the island's international house and techno communities. 🇮🇱 Israel The country's electronic-music and psytrance communities, including festival communities such as Doof Festival , as well as the wider dance-music culture surrounding Tel Aviv and beyond. 🌎 And Beyond The Recovery Kernel is equally relevant to communities surrounding: Tomorrowland Sónar MUTEK and countless local festivals, warehouse parties, clubs, circuit events, beach gatherings, sound-system cultures, and underground dance communities around the world. 🎛️ Why the Dancefloor Matters Dance culture is often discussed from two extremes. One side says: Just say no. The other says: Everyone does it. You'll be fine. Neither statement contains enough information to describe a human nervous system. People attending the same event can have radically different experiences. The same substance does not necessarily produce the same response in every person. The same weekend does not produce the same recovery timeline. The same environment does not create the same risk. The same behavior does not emerge from the same architecture. The Recovery Kernel exists in that space. Not to tell people how to party. Not to pretend risk does not exist. Not to pretend nightlife is inherently pathological. And not to demand that people abandon music, community, sexuality, movement, travel, or celebration in order to deserve understanding. The question is: What does this particular human system need us to understand? 💃 Recovery Does Not Have to Mean Exile From Joy For some people, traditional recovery culture can feel like an instruction to disappear from the world they knew. Leave the music. Leave the friends. Leave the nightlife. Leave the dancefloor. Leave sexuality. Leave celebration. Leave every environment associated with the former self. Sometimes distance from a particular environment is necessary. Sometimes it is lifesaving. But the larger goal of recovery should not automatically be permanent exile from joy. A person may need to learn: what environments destabilize them; what biological vulnerabilities they carry; what substances create disproportionate risk; what behavioral loops precede loss of control; what social conditions increase vulnerability; what recovery actually feels like in their own nervous system; and how to build a life in which pleasure does not automatically become self-destruction. The Recovery Kernel is interested in that question. How does a person remain alive enough to keep hearing the music? How do they understand themselves well enough to know when the dancefloor is joy — and when it has become a warning? How do we help people return to life without demanding that life become colorless? That is why the dancefloor belongs inside the Recovery Kernel. Because recovery is not merely the absence of a substance. It is the return of a person to their own life. 🌍 A Global Framework Addiction does not speak one language. Neither should recovery information. The Recovery Kernel project has been developed around a principle of global accessibility, with multilingual documentation and audio resources forming part of the broader project. 🌐 Global & Regional English English — Global Australian English Indian English Nigerian Pidgin — Naijá 🌹 Romance Languages French Spanish — Castilian Mexican Spanish Brazilian Portuguese European Portuguese Italian Catalan Galician 🏔️ Germanic & Nordic Languages German — Hochdeutsch Dutch Swedish Norwegian — Bokmål Danish 🧭 Slavic, Uralic & Other European Languages Polish Czech Bosnian Greek Turkish Finnish Basque — Euskara Irish — Gaeilge 🕌 Middle East & Central Asia Arabic — Modern Standard Hebrew Persian / Farsi Dari 🌏 South & Southeast Asia Hindi Bengali Indonesian Malay Burmese Thai Vietnamese Filipino / Tagalog 🏯 East Asia Chinese — Simplified Japanese Korean 🌍 African Languages Afrikaans Zulu — isiZulu Xhosa — isiXhosa Swahili — Kiswahili Hausa Yoruba Igbo The broader project also includes multilingual audiobook distribution designed to make the material usable beyond the written page. 📚 A Growing Recovery Library The Recovery Kernel is more than one book. It is an evolving library of tools and frameworks addressing areas such as: neurogenomics; substance-specific education; harm reduction; pharmacological interactions; recovery pathways; behavioral architecture; community safety; embodied wellness; movement and dance; genomic diversity; biohacking education; pharmacogenomic questions; multilingual accessibility. The project has included guides addressing multiple substance categories and recovery contexts, along with special resources for community safety, genomic interpretation, and embodied wellness. 💃 Recovery Is Also Embodied Recovery is not merely an intellectual exercise. Human beings move. Dance. Breathe. Touch the ground. Hear rhythm. Form communities. Experience pleasure. The Recovery Kernel project recognizes that recovery can involve more than avoiding a substance. It can also involve learning how to inhabit life again. That is why the larger library includes material exploring: movement; rhythm; nervous-system regulation; grounding; community connection; celebration; joy; safer social environments. The purpose is not to create another culture of permanent punishment. It is to help make room for life. 🛠️ Tools & Resources 🧬 DNA Estimation Estimate a preliminary DNA-related profile without a physical test: https://tinyurl.com/eab3k3nf When completing phenotype-based estimation, consider answering from the state in which the relevant pattern was most strongly expressed rather than only from an optimized or recovered state. Remember: phenotype estimation is probabilistic and cannot substitute for actual genomic testing. ⚠️ Interaction Checker Explore prescription, substance-risk, and pharmacogenomic interaction information: https://tinyurl.com/3y47pwtw Interaction information should be used to support informed conversations with qualified medical professionals, pharmacists, and emergency services where appropriate. 🍹 The Mocktail Prescriber The project includes The Bartender's Friend Mocktail Prescriber , an experimental framework designed to connect personal profile information with functional, non-alcoholic beverage concepts. For best personalization, genomic information may provide additional input beyond phenotype estimation. 🧪 Peptide Advisor & BioHacker Routine Generator Peptide Advisor https://tinyurl.com/ms9msj78 BioHacker Edition https://tinyurl.com/2b2eykpd These tools are educational. Peptides and experimental biohacking compounds can involve meaningful uncertainty, quality-control concerns, contraindications, and medical risk. Clinical involvement and qualified medical guidance are strongly recommended. 🎧 Free Audiobook Editions The project includes free audiobook resources for people who: prefer listening; have difficulty reading long documents; are traveling; are exercising; have visual-accessibility needs; learn better through audio. YouTube https://www.youtube.com/@J.R.Token.TheArchitect Listen while walking. Listen while sitting outside. Listen while rebuilding. The format is less important than making the information accessible. 📖 Paperback Edition For people who prefer a physical book: https://amazon.com/dp/B0GCVGTWQ8 A physical edition offers an alternative to screens, mobile devices, consoles, and constant digital distraction. Read somewhere quiet. Sit outside. Breathe fresh air. Take what is useful. Leave what is not. Return when you are ready. ☕ Support the Project The Recovery Kernel is designed around open access and broad availability. People who find the project useful can support its continuation here: https://buymeacoffee.com/jrtoken Another form of support: Consider donating books or educational materials to local prisons, recovery communities, shelters, or other places where access to information is limited. Knowledge should not belong only to people with money, perfect insurance, a university login, or a stable life. 🧑‍💻 Open Source Philosophy The Recovery Kernel is built around: Transparency Models and assumptions should be visible enough to examine and challenge. Accessibility Useful knowledge should be understandable outside professional institutions. Dignity People deserve explanations that do not begin with humiliation. Forkability Communities should be able to adapt tools for their own contexts. Global Reach Language should not be a gatekeeper to understanding. Bias Awareness Human reports, datasets, models, and AI outputs all have limitations. Community Participation People with lived experience are not merely research subjects. Their observations can help reveal where existing models fail. Scientific Curiosity A framework must be allowed to evolve when better evidence appears. 🤝 Who Is This For? The project may be useful to: Individuals People attempting to understand their own patterns, biology, triggers, or recovery experience. Families and Supporters People trying to understand what someone they care about may be experiencing. Developers People interested in building accessible health-education, genomics, recovery, visualization, translation, or AI systems. Researchers People exploring neurogenomics, behavior, recovery diversity, environmental interaction, or computational models. Recovery Communities Groups looking for non-moralizing language and adaptable educational frameworks. Clinicians and Pharmacists Professionals interested in seeing the kinds of questions people are attempting to answer outside traditional systems. Translators and Accessibility Contributors People who can help make knowledge available across languages, cultures, literacy levels, and media formats. 🌎 Why I Am Sharing This A lot of people do not connect with traditional recovery language. Some feel judged. Some feel misunderstood. Some have heard the same explanation for years and still do not understand what is happening inside them. Some want language that explains the brain and body without adding moral weight. Some are simply trying to survive long enough to understand themselves. That is why I am sharing this. Not because one framework contains every answer. Not because every hypothesis will survive forever unchanged. Not because software can replace human care. I am sharing it because people deserve access to tools that help them ask better questions about their own lives. If one person finds clarity here, then sharing it was worth it. Take care of yourselves. Read what is useful to you right now. Come back to the rest when you are ready. 🌐 How This Changes the Lens The Recovery Kernel attempts to move the conversation: MORAL FAILURE → BIOLOGICAL + BEHAVIORAL ARCHITECTURE SHAME → UNDERSTANDING CONFUSION → STRUCTURED QUESTIONS ANECDOTE → EVIDENCE + CONTEXT STIGMA → CURIOSITY JUDGMENT → INVESTIGATION "YOU FAILED" → "WHAT HAPPENED IN THE SYSTEM?" This framework is intended to be: humane scientifically curious bias-aware systems-oriented empowering non-judgmental open to correction 🔭 The Larger Vision Imagine a world where a person experiencing addiction can sit down and begin with: “Help me understand what could be happening.” Instead of: “Tell me why I am bad.” Imagine recovery systems where lived experience, pharmacology, genetics, environment, trauma, behavior, metabolism, and social context can be examined together rather than forced into competing silos. Imagine people arriving at professional care better able to: describe what happened; recognize patterns; communicate uncertainty; ask informed questions; identify contradictions; understand the difference between evidence and anecdote. That is the world the Recovery Kernel is trying to help build. ⚠️ Important Safety Notice The Recovery Kernel is an educational, open-source, and community resource framework. It does not replace: emergency medical services; physicians; pharmacists; mental-health professionals; addiction specialists; laboratory testing; individualized diagnosis or treatment. Some project materials discuss substances, withdrawal, interactions, experimental compounds, and recovery. Withdrawal from certain substances can be medically dangerous. Suspected overdose, severe withdrawal, breathing difficulty, loss of consciousness, seizure, severe confusion, or other acute medical emergencies require immediate professional assistance. United States emergency and crisis resources Emergency Services: 911 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Call or text 988 SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357 Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741741 Outside the United States, contact the appropriate emergency or crisis service in your country. 📬 Contact JR Token — The Architect Email: jr.token.thearchitect@gmail.com Audiobooks: https://www.youtube.com/@J.R.Token.TheArchitect Project Support: https://buymeacoffee.com/jrtoken 🙏 Acknowledgments The Recovery Kernel exists because of contributions from many forms of knowledge: people with lived experience; recovery advocates; researchers; neuroscientists; developers; data scientists; translators; harm-reduction practitioners; families; community health workers; accessibility advocates; open-source communities; and the people who kept asking questions after simple answers failed them. This work is also a product of an unusual collaboration between human observation, software engineering, structured knowledge systems, and multiple artificial-intelligence models. The project is intended to remain open to criticism, correction, iteration, and improvement. 🧬 THE RECOVERY KERNEL People are not error messages. Behavior has architecture. Architecture can be studied. Understanding can replace shame. When people understand their architecture, they can stop interpreting every struggle as a character defect. When shame loses its grip, curiosity becomes possible. When curiosity becomes possible, people can begin rebuilding. The Kernel is not a cure. It is not a treatment. It is not a protocol. It is a framework for understanding. And understanding is the beginning of everything. THE RECOVERY KERNEL OPEN SOURCE · FORKABLE · GLOBAL · BIAS-AWARE · HUMAN-FIRST Explore. Learn. Question. findings.title: DTIC ADA606650: Experimental Validation of the First 1-MA Water-Insulated Mykonos LTD Voltage Adder
findings.creator: Defense Technical Information Center
findings.description: The LTD technological approach can result in very compact devices that can deliver fast, high current and high voltage pulses straight out of the cavity without any complicated pulse forming and pulse-compression network. Through multistage inductively insulated voltage adders, the output pulse, increased in voltage amplitude, can be applied directly to the load. Because the output pulse rise time and width can be easily tailored (pulse shaped) to the specific application needs, the load may be a vacuum electron diode, a z-pinch wire array, a gas puff, a liner, an isentropic compression load (ICE) to study material behavior under very high magnetic fields, or a fusion energy (IFE) target. Ten 1-MA LTD cavities were originally designed and built to run in a vacuum or Magnetic Insulated Transmission Line (MITL) voltage adder configuration and, after successful operation in this mode, were modified and made capable to operate assembled in a de-ionized water insulated voltage adder. Special care has been taken to de-aerate the water and eliminate air bubbles. Our motivation is to test the advantages of water insulation compared to the MITL transmission approach. The desired effect is that the vacuum sheath electron current losses and pulse front erosion would be avoided without any new difficulties caused by the de-ionized water insulator. Presently, we have assembled and are testing a two-cavity, water insulated voltage adder with a liquid resistor load. Experimental results of up to 95kV capacitor charging are presented and compared with circuit code simulations.

findings.title: LO QUE EL MAR DEVUELVE III EL LEGADO DE TARSIS EDICION DIGITAL
findings.description: • La búsqueda del metal de los dioses: El episodio narra la trepidante carrera contra la organización Nexus por localizar la Nave Real Gaulós, un pecio fenicio del año 580 aC cargado de oricalco, una aleación legendaria tan valiosa que los antiguos la vinculaban con la Atlántida. • Tecnología de vanguardia y espionaje global: Acompaña al equipo de la Fundación Barrows en una misión que utiliza desde la constelación de satélites "Icarus", capaces de leer matrículas desde el espacio, hasta el hackeo de redes sismográficas para tesoros triangulares en el fondo marino. • Persecución en tres continentes: La trama se despliega desde los paisajes marcianos de las Minas de Riotinto en Huelva y la Nápoles sumergida, pasando por el lujo corrupto de Mykonos hasta las peligrosas aguas de la Triple Frontera en Sudamérica. • Inmersión extrema y ciencia ficción real: Descubre el desafío de bajar a 600 metros de profundidad mediante la ventilación líquida, una técnica experimental donde los protagonistas deben dejar de respirar aire para llenar sus pulmones de fluido oxigenado y sobrevivir a la presión del abismo. • El legado que reescribe la historia: El verdadero hallazgo de Tarsis no resulta ser el oro, sino una biblioteca sumergida con mapas de navegación que prueban que los fenicios llegaron a América mil años antes que Colón.

findings.title: ERIC ED569135: Shedding Light: Private "For Profit" Training Providers and Young Early School Leavers. NCVER Research Report
findings.description: This research investigates the oft-criticised segment of the vocational education and training (VET) sector in Australia--private, for-profit registered training organisations (RTOs)--with the aim of gaining a clearer understanding of the approaches they adopt in training 15 to 19-year-olds who have left school early. Through a nationwide survey of private RTOs and a series of consultations with providers and industry stakeholders in Victoria, South Australia, and Queensland, the authors set out to reveal the nature of training provided by private RTOs to those young people seeking to complete their initial qualification, and the ways by which they respond to the needs of their young learners. On the basis of the findings, changes are considered that may be needed in order to improve the training outcomes for this growing cohort of learners. The research is set against a background of federal, state, and territory-based training entitlement regimes, which ensure a greater role for the VET sector in supporting the initial qualification attainment of young Australians. It has also been undertaken at a time when state and national governments are promoting a marketised and, consequently, highly competitive provider environment, prompted largely by the 2012 National Agreement for Skills and Workforce Development and the National Partnership Agreement on Skills Reform. These initiatives saw an expansion in both the number of private RTOs accessing government-funding, which now comprise approximately 3000 of Australia's 4200 registered training providers, and the number of private RTOs delivering vocational education to early school leavers. In this context a convergence of two trends was observed: (1) a high number of private RTOs that often lack the infrastructure, economies of scale, and student supports found in TAFE (technical and further education) institutions; and (2) a high number of young early school leavers relying on such providers to help them to renew or continue their education. While the numbers of young people undertaking vocational education have increased, the completion rates of publicly subsidised courses remain very low. Data from the National Centre for Vocational Education Research (NCVER) indicate that, for those aged under 25 years in full-time study with no prior post school qualification, the estimated completion rate is 51.6% (NCVER 2016). This suggests that catering to the needs of young people in VET--across all provider types and settings--remains a significant challenge. It is for this reason that the focus is on the private RTOs, who now represent a prominent segment of the VET landscape. The following are appended: (1) Survey Instrument; (2) Sample Provider Profiles; (3) Semi-Structured Interview Instrument: Private RTOs; and (4) Semi-Structured Interview Instrument: Other Stakeholders.
